analysis.one_liner: Bans most noncompete agreements that stop workers from taking a new job in their field.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban most noncompete agreements was referred to the Senate labor committee in February 2023 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Roughly one in five American workers has signed a noncompete agreement, a contract clause that bars them from working for a competitor after they leave a job. This bill would make such agreements unenforceable, with narrow exceptions when someone sells a business or when a top executive leaves as part of a sale. It would let the Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Labor enforce the ban, and let workers and state attorneys general sue violators. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers covered by noncompete agreements — about one in five workers across income brackets and industries, by the bill's own findings — would gain the freedom to switch jobs, negotiate raises, or start businesses without legal threat. Consumers and job-seekers would also benefit from a more mobile, more innovative labor market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The one in five workers bound by noncompetes

how_it_helps.text: It voids noncompete agreements between employers and workers, so employees can take a better job or start a competing business without being sued.
It gives workers and state attorneys general the right to sue violators, with damages and attorney's fees, and blocks employers from forcing these disputes into arbitration or class-action waivers.
It preserves trade secret and nondisclosure protections, so employers can still protect genuinely confidential information.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use noncompete agreements to retain staff and suppress wage competition would lose that leverage, facing FTC and Labor Department enforcement, private lawsuits, and state attorney general actions.

drawbacks.text: Employers lose a tool they use to protect investments in training and customer relationships; the bill's answer is that trade secrets, intellectual property, and nondisclosure agreements already cover those legitimate interests, but some employers would face higher turnover costs.

The bill carves out exceptions for business sellers and for highly paid senior executives leaving in a sale, so the restrictions that matter most to companies would remain available at the top of the pay scale.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — workers free to change jobs and likely to earn more — is large and well documented in the bill's own findings; the main cost is that employers lose one blunt tool for keeping staff, and would have to lean on trade secrets and nondisclosure agreements, which the bill preserves. Narrow exceptions for business sellers and top executives limit the disruption to legitimate business sales. The bill died without ever being considered, so none of these tradeoffs was actually weighed on the record.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 1, 2023 and read twice, then referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That referral was the last action of any kind recorded on the bill; no hearing, markup, or vote followed during the two-year Congress.
The bill had three cosponsors from both parties, including two Republicans, but never reached the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on noncompete agreements to limit worker mobility and wage competition are better off, since the ban never advanced.

for.name: Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban most noncompete agreements.

for.name: Todd Young and Kevin Cramer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the ban, giving it Republican support.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three cosponsors included two Republicans alongside two Democrats, but no member of either chamber ever voted on it.

industries.note: The bill voids noncompetes for ordinary employees, removing a tool employers use to hold down turnover and wages. Employers would still have trade secrets and NDAs for genuinely confidential information.

Noncompetes remain allowed when selling a business and, for up to one year, for top executives leaving as part of a sale with severance pay. These carve-outs keep the ban from disrupting business transactions.
